title: Freight broker sales objections: understand the concern before responding.
seoTitle: Freight broker sales objections: understand the concern before responding
searchIntent: How should freight brokers respond to shipper objections and customer-routed freight?
excerpt: Separate a service concern from a buying-authority problem, including situations where the customer controls transportation.
takeaway: Ask enough to understand the objection. Then decide whether there is a service problem you can address or no purchasing opportunity at that contact.

sections.title: Find the concern behind the first answer.
paragraphs: Luis’s objection-handling lesson begins with diagnosis. A statement such as not wanting to use brokers can reflect cost, an earlier service failure, a communication problem, or a lack of authority to make the decision. Responding before understanding the reason can miss the actual concern.

His approach is to ask clarifying questions rather than immediately rebutting the answer. Follow the explanation far enough to understand what happened and why it matters to the prospect. The goal is a relevant conversation, not winning an argument about brokers in general.

sections.title: Connect the response to an actual service problem.
paragraphs: In one example, the initial concern is that brokers cost more. The discussion then reveals difficulty getting responses and dealing with missed pickups. That creates a more useful question: what coordination work would make the transportation arrangement easier to manage?

A response about service should be specific to what you can provide. Luis emphasizes arranging alternatives and handling the recovery work that otherwise falls on the shipper. Do not simply deny that brokerage has a commercial cost or promise that your operation can solve every interruption.

sections.title: Recognize customer routing as a real arrangement.
paragraphs: The customer-routed-freight lesson introduces a different situation. The company you are calling may sell the goods while its buyer controls transportation from the facility. The employee can be accurately describing the business arrangement rather than trying to avoid your pitch.

Luis uses a machine-manufacturer example to show the choice: the seller may arrange transportation, or the buyer may arrange collection. Before discussing a freight opportunity, establish which party makes that decision for the movement in question.

sections.title: Ask who controls each direction of freight.
paragraphs: Inbound and outbound arrangements can differ. A company might control transportation for one kind of movement and not another. Ask about the relevant flows without assuming that a single answer describes the entire operation.

If the contact does not buy transportation, identify whether there is another appropriate internal contact or a different movement it does control. Do not demand confidential customer information. An organization’s supply-chain arrangement is something to understand, not an objection that must always be overcome.

sections.title: Use appropriate persistence.
paragraphs: Luis includes persistence and finding actual decision authority in his broader framework. These work best when they produce new information. A different role may clarify responsibility, but contacting someone else should not involve disguising the earlier conversation or ignoring a request to stop.

Repeatedly giving the same response to the same refusal is not the same as learning. Ask whether the concern is clear, whether your service addresses it, and whether the person can act. If one of those conditions is absent, another sales pitch may not move the situation forward.

sections.title: Keep useful research even when there is no opportunity.
paragraphs: A call can still teach you product vocabulary and how an industry moves freight. The customer-routing lesson mentions pipeline pieces and valves as examples of information that can guide subsequent research. That does not require turning the contact into a source of private customer names.

Use what you legitimately learned to select better prospects and prepare better questions. Sometimes the correct next step is another conversation with this business. Sometimes it is moving on to a business whose needs and purchasing authority fit your service.
